Female Smalltail sharks (Carcharhinus porosus) attain a maximum total length of 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters], a figure that distinguishes them as somewhat smaller than many congeners within the coastal carcharhinid assemblage. At birth, neonates typically emerge at a total length of 32 centimeters [Lb = 32 centimeters], though field surveys have documented a range from 31 to 40 centimeters, suggesting modest variation attributable to maternal condition or gestational environment. Puberty in females is reached at approximately 70 centimeters [Lp = approximately 70 centimeters] total length, a size threshold that marks the onset of ovarian maturation and the capacity for gamete fusion. This length-based schedule of reproductive development is consistent with patterns observed in other small-bodied carcharhinids inhabiting the western Atlantic, where body size often serves as a reliable predictor of reproductive status.

At a stable water temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], the gestation period of Smalltail sharks lasts roughly 305 days [ab = roughly 305 days], representing the interval from fertilization to live birth. Following copulation and clasper-mediated fertilisation, the intrauterine embryo develops for approximately ten months before parturition, a duration typical of viviparous sharks that maintain a placental connection. This protracted gestational period, recorded under controlled laboratory conditions, reflects the substantial investment in offspring size at birth. The neonatal size of 32 centimeters [Lb = 32 centimeters] total length is relatively large compared to the maternal length at puberty, suggesting that females allocate considerable resources to individual pups rather than maximizing litter quantity within a single reproductive event.

Females produce litters ranging from 2 to 7 pups [N_R_i = litters ranging from 2 to 7 pups], and they typically deliver a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year] when maintained at 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. This annual cycle of reproductive activity is synchronized with seasonal environmental cues, and the combination of moderate litter size and annual frequency results in a modest lifetime reproductive output relative to more fecund teleosts. Gravid female sharks are regularly encountered in coastal nursery grounds, where the shallow waters provide shelter for pups during their first exogenous feeding and early juvenile development. The transition from yolk-sac resorption to independent foraging onset marks a critical period of heightened mortality for pups, underscoring the selective advantage of birth at a relatively advanced developmental stage.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females is approximately 6900 grams [Wwi = approximately 6900 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship typically applied to carcharhinid sharks. This asymptotic mass corresponds to the maximum body size recorded for the species and is achieved after females have completed their somatic growth phase and entered the reproductively active adult stage. The relationship between length and mass follows a power function in which weight increases disproportionately with total length, a pattern common among elasmobranchs and linked to their cartilaginous skeletons and lipid-rich livers. Sub-adult and juvenile sharks exhibit rapid mass gain during their early years, gradually decelerating as they approach their ultimate dimensions. This growth trajectory allows young individuals to pass through the vulnerable pup stage relatively quickly before attaining sizes that offer greater refuge from predation.

Maximum lifespan estimates for Carcharhinus porosus, derived from back-calculated ages of vertebral bands, indicate that individuals can live for 12 years [am = 12 years] under typical thermal conditions of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. This longevity is modest compared to larger carcharhinids such as Carcharhinus leucas, which may exceed 25 years, but is consistent with the life-history pace of smaller coastal sharks that experience higher natural mortality rates. The oldest documented individuals in field collections have been reproductively senescent females, suggesting that senescence-related physiological deterioration may limit lifespan beyond this value. Age-related death appears to follow the completion of several reproductive cycles, with late-stage individuals showing reduced body condition and worn claspers or reproductive tracts. This lifespan estimate anchors the species' demographic schedule and informs sustainable harvest models for artisanal fisheries in northern South America.
